docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Title Embedded Systems & IoT — Simplest to Complex Week Week 1 Date March 2026 Status Completed

docs.title: Task Description
docs.text: I was tasked with studying and explaining Embedded Systems and the Internet of Things (IoT) — starting from the most basic concepts and building up to more complex real-world applications. This included understanding what embedded systems are, how they interact with the physical world through sensors and actuators, and how IoT connects these devices over a network to enable smart, automated solutions.

docs.title: My Approach
docs.text:
1. I started by researching the fundamentals of embedded systems — understanding microcontrollers, basic input/output operations, and how hardware and software work together at a low level.
  2. I then studied IoT concepts, exploring how simple devices like temperature sensors and LEDs connect to more advanced systems such as smart home devices, industrial monitors, and network-connected controllers.
  3. Finally, I organized my findings from simplest to most complex — presenting a clear progression from a basic LED circuit all the way to a fully connected IoT network, demonstrating how each layer builds on the previous one.

docs.title: Reflection
docs.text:
What went well I was able to clearly understand and explain the progression from simple embedded components to complex IoT systems. Breaking it down step by step made the topic much easier to grasp. What was challenging Understanding how different communication protocols (like MQTT and HTTP) are used in IoT systems was initially difficult, as there were many options with different use cases. What I'd improve I would spend more time doing hands-on practice with actual hardware or simulation tools to reinforce the theoretical knowledge with practical experience.

Back to Assessments

docs.title: Assessment 2 — Connection Between PHP, IoT and Database
Overview
docs.text: Title Connection Between PHP, IoT and Database Week Week 2 Date March 2026 Status Completed

docs.title: Task Description
docs.text: I was tasked with understanding and demonstrating how PHP, IoT devices, and a database can work together as a complete system. The goal was to show how data collected by IoT sensors can be sent to a server, processed using PHP, and stored in a database — creating a full data pipeline from physical device to digital storage.

docs.title: My Approach
docs.text:
1. I started by understanding the role of each component — IoT devices collect real-world data (such as temperature or motion), PHP acts as the server-side language that receives and processes that data, and the database (MySQL) stores it for later retrieval or display.
  2. I then studied how an IoT device sends data to a PHP script via HTTP requests (GET or POST), and how the PHP script validates and inserts that data into a MySQL database table.
  3. Finally, I put it all together by mapping the full flow: IoT sensor → HTTP request → PHP script → MySQL database → data displayed on a web page, showing how each layer depends on and communicates with the next.

docs.title: Reflection
docs.text:
What went well I was able to clearly understand how the three technologies connect and depend on each other. The concept of a data pipeline from a physical sensor to a web interface became very clear once I mapped it step by step. What was challenging Understanding how to structure the HTTP request from the IoT device so that the PHP script could correctly receive and parse the data was initially confusing, especially handling different request methods. What I'd improve I would build a working prototype using an Arduino or Raspberry Pi sending real sensor data to a live PHP and MySQL server, to experience the full pipeline hands-on rather than just theoretically.

Back to Assessments

docs.title: Assessment 3 — Deploying Technical Documentation with MkDocs and GitHub Pages
Overview
docs.text: Title Deploying Technical Documentation with MkDocs and GitHub Pages Week Week 3 Date April 2026 Status Completed

docs.title: Task Description
docs.text: I was tasked with building and deploying a technical documentation site using MkDocs and hosting it publicly on GitHub Pages. The goal was to understand how modern documentation tools work, how to structure content in Markdown, configure a MkDocs project, and deploy it so anyone can access it through a live URL — without needing a traditional web server.

docs.title: My Approach
docs.text:
1. I started by installing MkDocs and the Material theme, then initialized a new project and explored the folder structure — understanding how mkdocs.yml controls the site configuration, navigation, theme, and plugins.
  2. I then wrote and organized the documentation content in Markdown files, configured the navigation in mkdocs.yml, and previewed the site locally using mkdocs serve to verify everything looked correct before publishing.
  3. Finally, I deployed the site to GitHub Pages using the mkdocs gh-deploy command, which automatically builds the site and pushes it to the gh-pages branch of the GitHub repository, making it publicly accessible via a GitHub Pages URL.

docs.title: Reflection
docs.text:
What went well The deployment process was straightforward once the project was properly configured. MkDocs and GitHub Pages work very well together, and seeing the live site go public after a single command was a great experience. What was challenging Configuring the mkdocs.yml file correctly — especially setting up navigation, enabling extensions, and making sure all file paths were accurate — required careful attention to detail and several adjustments. What I'd improve I would explore setting up a GitHub Actions workflow to automatically redeploy the site whenever changes are pushed to the main branch, making the process fully automated.

Back to Assessments

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
• mkdocs new [dir-name] - Create a new project.
  • mkdocs serve - Start the live-reloading docs server.
  • mkdocs build - Build the documentation site.
  • mkdocs -h - Print help message and exit.
